extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method; scientists interested in methods of explanation and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on methods for explaining and resolving laws of nature into more general laws, with examples (Newton, Liebig, Faraday) illustrating when an explanation is valid and how to test and apply general laws. Emphasizes modes of deduction, elimination of circumstances, limits of experimental methods, and the predictive/heuristic value of successful explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of explaining laws
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three modes of explaining laws of causation: First, resolving the law of an effect of combined causes into the separate laws of the causes, together with the fact of their combination. Secondly, resolving the law which connects any two links, not proximate, in a chain of causation, into the laws which connect each with the intermediate links. Thirdly, resolving two or more (special laws) into one by showing that what is true in several classes of cases is true under some more general supposition they have in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate mode depending on whether the phenomenon arises from combined causes, from remote links in a causal chain, or from multiple classes of instances that share a common condition. Note the third mode subsumes special laws under a genuine general law and does not require inductive extension by the Method of Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve laws into more general (and sometimes more certain) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first two modes laws are resolved into laws more general than themselves and also into laws more certain (more universally true) than themselves; in the third case the partial laws are in fact the same as the general one, so no difference of certainty exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resolving laws, assess whether the resulting laws are genuinely more general and whether this increases certainty (first two modes) or merely expresses the same law in a broader form (third mode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive extension of science via resolution of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: By resolving special laws into more general ones, the range of deductive science is extended because the laws thus resolved may thenceforth be deduced demonstratively from the more general laws into which they are resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful resolution should allow demonstrative deduction of former special laws from the more general principles, thereby increasing explanatory power and unifying disparate phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical meaning of 'explanation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation (of a law of nature) means pointing out some more general phenomenon of which it is a partial exemplification, or some laws of causation which produce it by their joint or successive action; it often substitutes one mystery for another and does not necessarily remove ultimate mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate 'explanation' with providing an ultimate why; require that an explanation identify more general laws or causal collocations from which the special law follows deductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct sense of 'accounted for' and proper use of 'cause'
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'account for' a law of nature means to assign other laws more general, together with collocations, which being supposed, the partial law follows without additional supposition. It is a misuse to say a general law 'causes' a partial law; the partial law is a case of the general one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming that one law accounts for another, ensure you specify the general laws plus the collocations (conditions) that jointly yield the partial law; avoid language that misuses 'cause' to imply ontological generation rather than subsumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of extraneous circumstances by varied instances
rubrics_metrics.description: To eliminate a peculiar circumstance as the cause of a phenomenon, obtain instances from other parts of the universe (or from varied classes) where that circumstance is absent; if the law still holds, that circumstance is not the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek instances differing in the suspect circumstance (e.g., celestial vs. terrestrial observations to eliminate 'proximity to earth') so that the shared condition remaining points to the true causal factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method: raising special observations into general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A special and apparently precarious generalization may be converted, by masterly employment of the Deductive Method, into a law pervading all nature if it is shown to explain numerous detached generalizations of a more limited kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a proposed general law by whether it unifies and explains many previously isolated generalizations; explanatory breadth and unification are signs of a strong deductive generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the Method of Difference in complex substances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Difference cannot be rigorously employed where the properties of different kinds of substance are involved, because it is often impossible to isolate the property differences cleanly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In experiments involving heterogeneous materials, recognize that strict Method of Difference controls may be impossible; adopt deductive reasoning or other methods to compensate and be cautious in inferring general laws from mixed-substance cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting subtle laws requires cases where results aren't intermixed
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature may be of extremely special and limited character experimentally because its results are only detectable where they are not intermixed and blended with those of other laws; such cases are necessary to reveal the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify experimental or natural contexts in which interfering processes are minimal so the target law's effects stand out; these 'clean' instances enable discovery and testing of subtle laws (as with Liebig's chemical contagion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation of intermediate links to resolve complex laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex law connecting remote cause to effect can often be resolved by interpolating proximate causes (intermediate links) in the chain of causation and resolving the special law into those intermediate laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining a remote causal relation, search for proximate mechanisms or chemical/physical steps that mediate the effect; demonstrating these intermediate links strengthens explanatory plausibility (illustrated by Liebig's respiration theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine all cases presenting necessary conditions for a law
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law has been discovered or when new light has been thrown upon a known law by experiment, it is important to examine all cases which present the conditions necessary for bringing that law into action, as this process is fertile in demonstrations of special laws and explanations of empiricisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After establishing a law, survey diverse situations where its conditions obtain to find new instances, special consequences, or to falsify/confirm the law; this systematic search yields further demonstrations and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive application of general laws to locate new phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a general law is established (e.g., Faraday's law that movement of a conductor at right angles to a magnet evolves electricity), one may deduce where analogous conditions hold (e.g., streams, wheels) and predict new instances or explain phenomena (Aurora Borealis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use derived general principles to generate concrete predictions about where or when phenomena should occur; successful prediction is strong evidence of explanatory adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of empirical practices into simpler laws improves arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations on which the operations of the arts have been founded are continually justified and confirmed, or rectified and improved, by discovering the simpler scientific laws (chemical, physiological) on which their efficacy depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practical methods by whether they can be resolved into known scientific laws; doing so can justify, refine, or replace empirical practices with improved processes grounded in proximate causes (examples: agriculture, surgery, healing arts).
